title: DataHandler Is the Write Path for Records
hints: Every record change the backend makes goes through DataHandler. It evaluates the TCA of each field, checks the editor's permissions, keeps workspaces and localizations consistent and updates the reference index. A direct INSERT writes the row and none of that, so the record exists and nothing else about it is true.

DataHandler acts as a backend user: pass one to start() or have one in $GLOBALS['BE_USER']. Permission checks, workspaces and the reference index all hang off it, which is what makes DataHandler the right way to seed and a direct INSERT the wrong one.

The rest of the subject is its own hint, because each is asked as its own question: datahandler-writing for the datamap, datahandler-relations for a relation field, datahandler-placement for which page may hold a record and where it lands on it, datahandler-seeding for building content that exists nowhere yet, datahandler-testing for covering any of it. Reading records back is persistence-reading and works nothing like this.

title: Writing Records with a Datamap
hints: Writing records goes through a datamap: $dataMap[<table>][<uid or "NEW" plus a unique suffix>][<field>], handed to start($dataMap, $cmdMap) and then process_datamap(). Moving, copying and deleting go through the command map instead. A new record's real uid comes back in substNEWwithIDs, keyed by the placeholder.

title: What a Datamap Does to a Relation Field
hints: A relation field takes a comma-separated list of the related uids on the parent's own field, "NEW" placeholders included; those resolve once the children have been created in the same run. Where the field declares foreign_field, DataHandler writes the parent uid onto every child, together with foreign_table_field, foreign_match_fields and a sorting value counted up in list order. The parent's own column then holds the number of children rather than the list, as an MM field's column does. Only a relation stored in the parent column itself keeps the list, so a child's pointer column and a parent's counter are never written by hand.

A placeholder in that list may carry no underscore. DataHandler::processRemapStack() splits such a value on "_" as the <table>_<uid> notation, so NEW_card1 is looked up as "card1" and resolves to nothing, and RelationHandler::readList() then discards what is left. Nothing reports it: the run finishes clean, the error log stays empty, the children exist as rows, and the parent's counter stays 0 with uid_foreign never set on them. StringUtility::getUniqueId('NEW') produces an id that always conforms. The constraint is on what a relation field is handed rather than on the placeholder itself, so a datamap key, a -NEW... positioning pid and an MM parent id take an underscore.

This is the write side. What the parent field and the child table have to declare before any of it is a child relation — the parent column, what orders the children, the page types the rows may sit on — is tca-inline-children.

title: Which Page May Hold a New Record, and Where It Lands on It
hints: Which page may hold the record is settled before it is positioned, and getting it wrong costs the record quietly: DataHandler refuses the insert, writes a log entry and carries on, so the run raises nothing and the row is not there. A standard page allows pages, sys_category, sys_file_reference, sys_file_collection and the tables whose TCA declares ctrl.security.ignorePageTypeRestriction — that is how tt_content gets there. A folder, doktype 254, allows every table, which is what makes a storage folder the place a table of your own goes rather than an editorial habit.

Being an admin does not get past that: the doktype is checked after the permission check an admin and bypassAccessCheckForRecords short-circuit, so a seeding script running as the CLI user meets it in full.

A pid of 0 is the other question, and the table's own TCA answers it: ctrl.rootLevel is 0 for a table that lives on pages, 1 for one that only exists at the root and -1 for either, and an insert at the root needs an admin or ctrl.security.ignoreRootLevelRestriction on top. pages is exempt and goes anywhere.

hints.text: Which tables a page type allows is declared in the pages TCA, as allowedRecordTypes on that page type; PageDoktypeRegistry reads it from there.
Which tables a page type allows is declared in PageDoktypeRegistry itself, and an extension changes it with add() or addAllowedRecordTypes().

hints: A new record is placed at the TOP of its page: the pid field is the positioning pid, and a page uid there means "first record on that page". A datamap written in reading order therefore comes out reversed — pages in a menu, content elements in a column.

To place records in order, use the negative form: a pid of -<uid> means "directly after that record". A "NEW" placeholder may be used there as well, as -NEW..., and resolves once the record it names has been created in the same run.

title: Seeding Records with a Script
hints: A page tree that has to be established again — on the next installation, in a fresh environment, after a reset — is what impexp is for: the exported T3D or XML is the artifact, impexp:import puts it back into a page tree, and extension:setup does the same for a package that ships one. Seed with a script for content that exists nowhere yet, then export it. sitepackage-initial-content is the shipping half.

No console command hands you a DataHandler, so seeding is a script that boots TYPO3 itself. Bootstrap::init($classLoader), and nothing else: the second parameter is $failsafe, and the CLI binary passes it as true only because the command application finishes the boot afterwards. In failsafe mode the container is the reduced one, TCA is never built, and makeInstance() then constructs a core service itself with no arguments — so the failure reads as a constructor missing its arguments rather than as a service that is not registered.

Then the backend user, in that order: Bootstrap::initializeBackendUser(CommandLineUserAuthentication::class) creates it, Bootstrap::initializeBackendAuthentication() logs it in, and the second one alone has no $GLOBALS['BE_USER'] to check. Anything that reads a site attribute needs $GLOBALS['LANG'] as well, which the command application builds with LanguageServiceFactory::createFromUserPreferences($GLOBALS['BE_USER']).

In one datamap the pages are processed before every other table, so a record whose pid is the NEW id of a page created in the same call still lands on it. Between two other tables the order of the datamap decides, and a NEW id that has not been substituted yet leaves that record unwritten — a log entry, no exception. Where the target is not a page, create it in a first process_datamap() call, read substNEWwithIDs, and pass real ids in the second.

A NEW id carries no underscore. processRemapStack() splits one on the last underscore and reads what is in front of it as a table name, so a relation field naming NEWid_one substitutes nothing: the child is written, the parent field stays empty or counts zero, and nothing is logged. NEWidOne is the same id without the trap.

A field that is not a relation substitutes nothing either, whatever it holds. A link written as t3://page?uid=NEWpage keeps that string, so a value that has to name a record created in the same script is written in a second call, from substNEWwithIDs.

A new record takes the default its TCA field declares, and that is not the default its column carries: pages.hidden is 1 in TCA against 0 in the schema, so a page tree seeded without saying otherwise is written hidden. Nothing reports it, the export ships it as it is, and the receiving installation answers not found on every page of that tree, its root included. page-not-found-within-a-site is the same fact from the failing request's end, where the exclamation mark on that message is what says the page was found and withheld.

title: Testing DataHandler Behaviour
hints: DataHandler and persistence changes are high-impact and usually need functional tests.
Preserve workspace, localization, permissions, and hook or event behavior unless intentionally changed.
Test edge cases with deleted, hidden, localized, versioned, or workspace records when relevant.

hints.text: DataHandler scenarios extend AbstractDataHandlerActionTestCase instead of FunctionalTestCase; it carries the scenario setup those tests share. It lives in typo3/sysext/core/Tests/Functional/DataScenarios/, which is the core's own test tree — an extension writes an ordinary FunctionalTestCase and primes its records with CSV fixtures.
